metadata.title: A/B Tests Can Lie.
metadata.topic: A/B TESTING · SAMPLE RATIO MISMATCH · PEEKING · PYTHON
source: Fabijan A, Gupchup J, Gupta S, Omhover J, Qin W, Vermeer L, Dmitriev P. Diagnosing Sample Ratio Mismatch in Online Controlled Experiments: A Taxonomy and Rules of Thumb for Practitioners. KDD '19. doi:10.1145/3292500.3330722 (authors' version in sources/: §1 + §5.3 MSN carousel 12→16, significant decrease, SRM, bot filter removed most-engaged treatment users, flipped, shipped; §4.1 ~6% of Microsoft experiments exhibit an SRM; §2.3.1 821,588 vs 815,482 < 1 in 500k)

Johari R, Pekelis L, Walsh DJ. Always Valid Inference: Bringing Sequential Analysis to A/B Testing. arXiv:1512.04922v1 (2015) (App. C: continuous monitoring Type I error > 30% at 10,000 observations). Published: Operations Research 2022;70(3):1806–1821, doi:10.1287/opre.2021.2135 (not read)
py/carousel_v1.py, py/carousel_v2.py, py/peeking.py, py/abtest.py — simulations (Python 3.13.1 stdlib, fixed seeds); outputs in py/*.out
metadata.description: How an A/B test can look significant and still be wrong: a real MSN carousel test that read as a significant loss was a win — a bot filter had removed the most engaged users from one group (a sample ratio mismatch). Plus peeking: checking daily makes a quarter of no-difference tests crown a winner. Built with real Python simulations.
